CausalChain: DDR gene mutations → Excess DNA damage → Increased neoantigen production and cytosolic DNA accumulation → Activation of the STING pathway → Induction of type-I interferon response → Potential recruitment of effector T cells into the tumor microenvironment → Counter balance by TGF-β–mediated immunosuppression → Combination of DDR inhibitors, TGF-β blockers, and immune checkpoint inhibitors can reset the TME toward immunogenicity
Hypothesis: In BTCs, DDR deficiencies not only elevate tumor mutational burden but also activate the STING pathway to drive an innate interferon response; however, this immune stimulus is dampened by high TGF-β activity. Concurrent inhibition of TGF-β signaling along with DDR-targeted therapy and PD-1/PD-L1 blockade will synergistically reprogram the TME, enhancing immune cell infiltration and response to immunotherapy.
Abstract: Recent studies in biliary tract cancer (BTC) have highlighted the complex interplay between DNA damage repair (DDR) deficiencies, tumor mutational burden, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Although elevated DDR gene mutations may increase neoantigen load through the accumulation of mutations, BTCs often exhibit an immunologically ‘cold’ TME characterized by suppressive cellular elements and cytokines. We hypothesize that DDR abnormalities, by activating cytosolic DNA sensing pathways such as STING, can induce a type‐I interferon response that may remodel the TME toward a more immunogenic state. However, concomitant signaling through pathways such as TGF‐β—frequently upregulated in BTC—is likely to impede this immune activation. A combinatorial therapeutic approach targeting DDR defects, alleviating TGF‐β–mediated suppression and concurrently applying PD‐1/PD‐L1 immune checkpoint blockade may synergistically overcome immune resistance in a subset of BTC patients.
